title: Fiduciary duties and constructive trusts
subtitle: The no-conflict and no-profit rules, proprietary remedies, and the limits of the fiduciary label
objectives: Define a fiduciary relationship and state the core content of the no-conflict and no-profit rules as formulated in Bristol & West BS v Mothew

Explain why an honest fiduciary who benefits the person they act for can still be strictly liable to account for an unauthorised profit (Keech v Sandford; Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver; Boardman v Phipps), and how bribes and secret commissions are now recoverable proprietarily (FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital)

Apply the current test for who counts as a fiduciary to new fact patterns, and correctly identify when a duty to give disinterested advice does not, by itself, create a fiduciary relationship (Hopcraft v Close Brothers)

leadingAuthorities.citation: Keech v Sandford (1726) Sel Cas Ch 61
leadingAuthorities.role: Founding statement of the strict no-profit rule: a trustee who renews a trust lease for himself holds it on constructive trust, whatever his good faith
Directors liable to account for profit on shares acquired by virtue of their office, despite acting in good faith and benefiting the company
A fiduciary honestly acting for the trust's benefit is nonetheless strictly liable to account for an unauthorised profit made from the fiduciary position

leadingAuthorities.citation: Bristol & West Building Society v Mothew [1998] Ch 1
leadingAuthorities.role: Leading modern formulation of what a fiduciary is and the content of the no-conflict/no-profit duties of loyalty

leadingAuthorities.citation: FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC [2014] UKSC 45
leadingAuthorities.role: A bribe or secret commission received by a fiduciary is held on constructive trust — resolving the Reid/Sinclair split in favour of a proprietary remedy

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hopcraft v Close Brothers Ltd [2025] UKSC 33
leadingAuthorities.role: A duty to give disinterested advice does not, without more, make the adviser a fiduciary — car dealers acting as credit brokers owed no fiduciary duty on this basis

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can recite the no-profit rule but freeze the moment a fact pattern involves someone who acted honestly, or even helped the person they were supposed to be loyal to. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the rule is strict — this lesson is about applying it even when your instinct says the defendant doesn't deserve to lose.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the definitions here before. The test pool below is weighted towards fact patterns, including several designed to trigger sympathy for an 'innocent' fiduciary — apply the rule anyway.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state the Mothew formulation of the no-conflict and no-profit rules before moving on — Parts 3 to 5 assume you have it cold.

overview.hook: A trustee renews a lease for himself instead of the trust, because the landlord flatly refused to renew it for a child beneficiary. He does nothing dishonest, gains nothing he wasn't offered anyway, and still loses everything. Equity doesn't care why — and three centuries later, in a Supreme Court case decided this year, that same doctrine met its limit: a car dealer who had to give you disinterested advice about a loan turned out, after all, not to be your fiduciary at all.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. Flagged for currency: Hopcraft v Close Brothers Ltd [2025] UKSC 33 was decided by the Supreme Court very recently and materially reshapes the boundary of who counts as a fiduciary in commercial and consumer-facing relationships. Earlier materials that predate August 2025 will not reflect it, and some will assume — wrongly — that any duty to give disinterested advice is itself enough to found fiduciary status. This lesson states the law as clarified by Hopcraft.

parts.heading: What actually makes someone a fiduciary
parts.voice: definitional — precise and unsentimental about what loyalty requires in law
body: A fiduciary is someone who has undertaken to act for or on behalf of another in a particular matter, in circumstances that give rise to a relationship of trust and confidence. Trustees are the paradigm case, but the category reaches much further: company directors, agents, solicitors acting for clients, partners in a partnership, and others who have undertaken to act in another's interests rather than their own.

The single clearest modern statement of what this actually requires comes from Millett LJ in Bristol & West Building Society v Mothew: 'the distinguishing obligation of a fiduciary is the obligation of loyalty.' From that core obligation, two specific rules follow. The no-conflict rule: a fiduciary must not place themselves in a position where their own interest conflicts, or may conflict, with the interest of the person they act for. The no-profit rule: a fiduciary must not make an unauthorised profit from their position, even where no conflict of interest is otherwise apparent.

Millett LJ was equally precise about what a fiduciary duty is not: it is not simply a duty to take care, or to act competently — those are ordinary duties that anyone, fiduciary or not, may owe in contract or tort. A solicitor who is merely careless has breached a duty of skill and care, not necessarily a fiduciary duty. Confusing 'has a duty toward someone' with 'is that person's fiduciary' is the single most common error this lesson exists to correct — and, as Part 5 will show, it is exactly the error the Supreme Court had to unpick in 2025.

components.definition: A person who has undertaken to act for or on behalf of another in a particular matter in circumstances giving rise to a relationship of trust and confidence, and who therefore owes an obligation of single-minded loyalty — including the no-conflict and no-profit rules — going beyond an ordinary duty of care and skill.

interaction.prompt: According to Millett LJ in Bristol & West BS v Mothew, is a duty to act carefully and competently, by itself, the same thing as a fiduciary duty?
options: No — a duty of care is a distinct obligation; the fiduciary duty is specifically one of loyalty
Yes — any duty owed to another person in a professional capacity is automatically fiduciary
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Mothew is precise about this: carelessness breaches a duty of skill and care, not (without more) a fiduciary duty. The fiduciary obligation is specifically about loyalty — no conflict, no unauthorised profit.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — Mothew deliberately separates the two. A duty of care and a fiduciary duty of loyalty are different obligations, and a professional relationship does not automatically carry both. Keep this distinction in mind; it resurfaces sharply in Part 5.

parts.heading: Keech v Sandford: equity doesn't ask why
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story, then states the doctrine at its harshest
body: A trustee held a lease of a market on trust for a child beneficiary. When the lease came up for renewal, the trustee approached the landlord to renew it for the trust. The landlord refused — he did not want to grant a further lease to a child, or to any trust arrangement, at all. So the trustee, unable to renew for the beneficiary, renewed the lease for himself instead.

Lord King LC held that the trustee held the new lease on constructive trust for the beneficiary, exactly as if he had renewed it in the trust's name. It made no difference that the trustee had done nothing underhand, had not schemed for the renewal, and had only taken the lease because the landlord would not deal with the trust at all. The rule, as Lord King put it, had to be applied strictly, 'for it is very obvious what would be the consequence' if trustees were allowed to keep property acquired by virtue of their position whenever they could point to an innocent reason for doing so.

This is the doctrine at its most unforgiving, and it is deliberately unforgiving: the strictness is the point. If liability turned on proving bad faith, every trustee accused of self-dealing would simply assert an innocent motive, and courts would be drawn into exactly the kind of speculative inquiry into private intentions that equity's bright-line rule is designed to avoid. Keech is the founding statement of a principle the next part will watch operate at full strength against defendants who behaved impeccably.

components.factsShort: A trustee, unable to renew a trust lease for a child beneficiary because the landlord refused, renewed it for himself instead.
components.ratioShort: A trustee who renews a trust lease for their own benefit holds the new lease on constructive trust for the beneficiary, regardless of good faith or the landlord's refusal to deal with the trust.

expanded.facts: The trustee held a lease of Romford Market on trust for an infant. On approaching the landlord about renewal, he was told the landlord would not renew to the trust — only to the trustee personally, if at all. The trustee accepted a new lease in his own name.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord King LC held the new lease must be treated as held on trust for the infant beneficiary. Though he accepted there was 'no fraud' in the case, he considered it necessary that the rule 'be strictly pursued, and not in the least relaxed', because otherwise trustees would too readily be able to justify keeping property for themselves.
expanded.significance: Keech is the founding authority for the strict, motive-blind no-profit rule that runs through the whole of this lesson. It establishes that the remedy for breach is proprietary — a constructive trust over the very asset acquired — not merely a personal liability to pay damages, and that the rule applies even where enforcing it produces a result that looks, on the facts, entirely unfair to the trustee.

interaction.prompt: In Keech v Sandford, why did the trustee's good faith not prevent liability?
options: Because the no-profit rule is applied strictly regardless of the fiduciary's honesty or motive
Because the trustee had in fact acted fraudulently despite the court's finding
Because trustees can never personally hold a lease under any circumstances
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong turn is to assume the court must have found hidden dishonesty to justify the result — it explicitly did not. Lord King accepted there was no fraud and imposed liability anyway, precisely to keep the rule strict and free of case-by-case inquiries into motive.

parts.heading: Honest, helpful, and still liable: Regal (Hastings) and Boardman v Phipps
parts.voice: strict-liability — flat, procedural, refuses to let sympathy for the defendant soften the rule
body: In Regal (Hastings) Ltd v Gulliver, directors of a company arranged for a subsidiary to acquire two cinemas, but the company could not itself fund the purchase in full. The directors personally subscribed for the shortfall of shares, in good faith, to get a deal done that benefited the company. The company was later sold, the shares rose in value, and the directors profited. The House of Lords held the directors liable to account for that profit to the company — even though the company had suffered no loss, had benefited from the transaction, and the directors had acted honestly throughout. The profit was made by virtue of their fiduciary position; that was enough.

Boardman v Phipps pushed the same logic further and is the case most students find genuinely uncomfortable. A solicitor to a family trust, Boardman, used information and opportunities that came to him through acting for the trust to personally acquire shares in a company the trust already held a minority stake in. He acted throughout in good faith, kept the trustees broadly informed, and the investment turned out extremely well — it substantially benefited the trust's own shareholding as well as himself. The House of Lords held, by a narrow majority, that Boardman was nonetheless liable to account for his personal profit: he was in a fiduciary position, the opportunity and information came to him through that position, and he had not obtained the fully informed consent of every beneficiary before acting on it for himself.

Put the two cases together and the doctrine states itself: liability under the no-profit rule does not depend on dishonesty, on loss to the principal, or even on the principal benefiting from what the fiduciary did. It depends only on an unauthorised profit having been made from the fiduciary position. Equity doesn't ask why, and it doesn't ask whether things turned out well.

components.label: What the no-profit rule requires — and does not require
points: Requires only: a fiduciary position, and an unauthorised profit made by reason of (or by virtue of, or by use of information/opportunity arising from) that position
Does NOT require dishonesty or bad faith on the fiduciary's part (Keech; Regal (Hastings))
Does NOT require the principal to have suffered any loss (Regal (Hastings): the company was unharmed)
Does NOT require the principal to have been left worse off by the transaction overall (Boardman v Phipps: the trust's own holding benefited too)
Is displaced by fully informed consent from the principal (or, for trustees, all beneficiaries) authorising the profit in advance

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from the majority reasoning in Boardman v Phipps, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
interaction.passage: Boardman argued that he had acted honestly, kept the trustees informed, and that his actions had ultimately benefited the trust's own shareholding. The majority accepted all of this as true. Nonetheless, where a person in a fiduciary position obtains, by reason and in the course of that fiduciary position, a profit or advantage, he is liable to account for it to his principal, unless he has obtained the fully informed consent of his principal to retain it. Good faith and benefit to the principal go only to the question of what account should be taken, not to whether liability to account arises at all.
interaction.ratioSentence: Where a person in a fiduciary position obtains, by reason and in the course of that fiduciary position, a profit or advantage, he is liable to account for it to his principal, unless he has obtained the fully informed consent of his principal to retain it.

parts.heading: Bribes and secret commissions: the proprietary remedy
parts.voice: case-narrative — resolves a doctrinal split through the facts of the case that settled it
body: A particularly serious form of unauthorised profit is the bribe or secret commission: a fiduciary — an agent, most commonly — receives a payment from a third party in connection with a transaction they are handling for their principal, without disclosing it. For decades English law was split on how the principal could recover it. One line of authority (Sinclair Investments v Versailles) treated the claim as merely personal — a debt owed by the fiduciary, ranking alongside the fiduciary's other unsecured creditors if the fiduciary became insolvent. Another (following the Privy Council's Attorney General for Hong Kong v Reid) treated the bribe itself as held on constructive trust for the principal from the moment of receipt — a proprietary claim, giving the principal priority over the fiduciary's general creditors and a claim to any increase in the bribe's value.

The Supreme Court resolved the split in FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC. An agent negotiating the purchase of a hotel group for FHR received an undisclosed €10 million commission from the seller. The Supreme Court held unanimously that a bribe or secret commission received by a fiduciary in connection with their principal's affairs is held on constructive trust for the principal — resolving the split firmly in favour of the proprietary analysis, and overruling Sinclair Investments on this point.

The practical stakes of this are real, not academic: a personal claim is worthless against an insolvent fiduciary once other creditors are paid; a proprietary claim lets the principal trace and recover the actual asset — or its traceable proceeds — ahead of everyone else. FHR is now the standard starting point whenever a fiduciary has taken a bribe or secret commission, and it sits squarely within the no-profit principle traced through this lesson: the commission was an unauthorised profit made by virtue of the agent's fiduciary position, full stop.

components.caseName: FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC
components.factsShort: An agent negotiating a hotel purchase received an undisclosed €10 million commission from the seller, without his principal's knowledge.
components.ratioShort: A bribe or secret commission received by a fiduciary by reason of their fiduciary position is held on constructive trust for the principal, giving a proprietary — not merely personal — remedy.

expanded.facts: Cedar Capital acted as FHR's agent in negotiating the purchase of the share capital of a company owning the Monte Carlo Grand Hotel. Unknown to FHR, Cedar had also agreed a €10 million commission with the seller, payable on completion. FHR sought to recover the commission and argued it was held on constructive trust.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Neuberger, giving the judgment of a unanimous seven-justice panel, held that where an agent receives a bribe or secret commission, it is beneficially owned by the principal and is held by the agent on constructive trust. The court preferred this proprietary analysis over the competing 'merely personal debt' line of authority, for reasons including consistency, simplicity, and the practical unfairness of leaving a defrauded principal to compete with the fiduciary's other creditors.
expanded.significance: FHR is now the leading and binding authority on the remedy for bribes and secret commissions received by a fiduciary, resolving a long-running split between the Reid and Sinclair lines of authority. It confirms that this category of unauthorised profit attracts a proprietary constructive trust, with all the tracing and priority advantages that carries — reinforcing, rather than qualifying, the strict no-profit principle from Parts 2 and 3.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that makes FHR's proprietary constructive trust analysis (rather than a merely personal claim) the right remedy on these facts.
interaction.scenarioText: An agent is instructed to source a shipping contract for his principal. Unknown to the principal, the counterparty pays the agent a secret commission of £50,000 to secure the deal. The agent later becomes insolvent, with the £50,000 (now grown to £58,000 after being invested) traceable into a specific bank account.
tappableSpans: instructed to source a shipping contract
traceable into a specific bank account
interaction.correctSpan: traceable into a specific bank account
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right instinct, though note: FHR establishes the constructive trust arises the moment the bribe is received, regardless of insolvency. What insolvency and traceability change is why the proprietary analysis matters in practice — it lets the principal claim the traced, grown asset ahead of the agent's other creditors.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The constructive trust itself arises on receipt of the secret commission (that's the FHR holding), not because of insolvency. But look at what makes the proprietary remedy practically valuable here rather than just theoretically correct — it's the fact that the asset can be traced into a specific fund, ahead of unsecured creditors.

parts.heading: Hopcraft v Close Brothers: not every duty of loyalty makes you a fiduciary
parts.voice: corrective — steps back from the strictness of Parts 2 to 4 to mark where the fiduciary label actually stops
body: Everything so far might suggest the fiduciary label is easy to trigger and brutal once triggered. The Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Hopcraft v Close Brothers Ltd is the necessary corrective, and it belongs squarely alongside Mothew's warning in Part 1: a duty owed to someone is not automatically a fiduciary duty.

The case concerned car dealers acting as credit brokers, arranging finance for customers buying vehicles, and receiving commission from the lender for doing so — commission the customers were often not told about. Claimants argued that, because the broker had a duty to give the customer disinterested, unbiased advice about the finance options available, the broker was necessarily the customer's fiduciary — and that undisclosed commission was therefore an unauthorised fiduciary profit, on the same footing as Boardman's shares or Cedar Capital's commission in FHR.

The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning. A duty to act with a degree of disinterestedness, or to give balanced advice, does not by itself create the relationship of trust and confidence — the undertaking to subordinate your own interests entirely to the customer's — that fiduciary status actually requires. The dealers were in business selling cars and arranging finance on commercial terms; they had not undertaken the single-minded loyalty a fiduciary owes. This does not leave undisclosed commission unregulated — the Court's judgment also engaged the separate statutory route under the Consumer Credit Act 1974, s 140A, which lets a court intervene where a credit relationship between a lender and borrower is unfair, a distinct and more flexible remedy that does not depend on fiduciary status at all. But as a matter of fiduciary law specifically, Hopcraft draws the line squarely: disinterested advice, without an underlying undertaking of loyalty, is not enough.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often reason that any professional who is supposed to advise 'in your interest' or 'without bias' must be a fiduciary, and treat undisclosed commission in that relationship as automatically an unauthorised fiduciary profit.
components.whyItsWrong: Hopcraft v Close Brothers confirms that a duty to give disinterested advice is not, by itself, sufficient to establish a fiduciary relationship. Fiduciary status requires an undertaking of single-minded loyalty of the kind identified in Mothew — something more than a duty of fair or unbiased dealing within an otherwise ordinary commercial relationship. Get the threshold question wrong and the whole no-conflict/no-profit analysis from Parts 2 to 4 is being applied to a defendant who was never a fiduciary in the first place.

interaction.prompt: A mortgage broker is contractually required to recommend the mortgage product that best suits the customer's circumstances, from a panel of lenders. Unknown to the customer, the broker receives a higher commission from one particular lender on that panel, and recommends that lender's product. Applying Hopcraft v Close Brothers, does the broker owe the customer a fiduciary duty in respect of the undisclosed commission?
factsToOrder: The broker must recommend the best-suited product from a panel
The broker receives a higher commission from one lender on the panel
The customer is not told about the commission
The broker recommends the higher-commission lender's product
The relationship is a commercial broking arrangement, not an undertaking of general loyalty

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a mortgage broker under a duty to recommend the best-suited product owes the customer a fiduciary duty, such that undisclosed commission is recoverable as an unauthorised fiduciary profit.
modelAnswer.rule: Fiduciary status requires an undertaking of single-minded loyalty (Mothew); a duty to give disinterested or suitability-based advice does not, without more, create that relationship (Hopcraft v Close Brothers). Where fiduciary status is established, an unauthorised profit made by virtue of the position must be accounted for, and a secret commission is held on constructive trust (FHR European Ventures).
modelAnswer.application: The broker's duty to recommend a suitable product is closely analogous to the disinterested-advice duty in Hopcraft: it constrains how the broker must act within a commercial broking relationship, but it does not by itself amount to an undertaking to subordinate the broker's own interests entirely to the customer's, of the kind fiduciary status requires. Following Hopcraft, this duty alone is unlikely to make the broker a fiduciary, so the undisclosed commission is not automatically recoverable under the no-profit rule or FHR's constructive trust analysis. The customer is not without a remedy in principle — mis-selling, breach of regulatory duties, or an unfair relationship analysis akin to Consumer Credit Act 1974, s 140A may be available — but those are separate causes of action from a fiduciary claim.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On Hopcraft's reasoning, the broker most likely does not owe a fiduciary duty merely by virtue of the suitability obligation, so a fiduciary no-profit claim over the undisclosed commission is unlikely to succeed, even though other legal routes may still be open to the customer.

testPool.prompt: Name the two core duties Millett LJ identified as the content of a fiduciary's obligation of loyalty in Bristol & West BS v Mothew.
acceptableAnswers: the no-conflict rule and the no-profit rule
no conflict of interest and no unauthorised profit
testPool.modelAnswer: The no-conflict rule (a fiduciary must not place themselves in a position where their own interest conflicts, or may conflict, with the interest of the person they act for) and the no-profit rule (a fiduciary must not make an unauthorised profit from their position).

testPool.prompt: In Keech v Sandford, could the trustee keep the renewed lease because the landlord had refused to renew it to the trust?
options: No — he held it on constructive trust for the beneficiary regardless
Yes — the landlord's refusal excused the trustee

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is required to establish liability under the no-profit rule?
options: Proof that the fiduciary acted dishonestly
An unauthorised profit made by virtue of the fiduciary position, without more
Proof that the principal suffered a financial loss
testPool.trapExplanation: Regal (Hastings) and Boardman v Phipps both establish that neither dishonesty nor loss to the principal is required — the rule is strict, and turns only on an unauthorised profit having been made from the fiduciary position.

testPool.prompt: In Hopcraft v Close Brothers Ltd [2025] UKSC 33, did the Supreme Court hold that credit brokers were fiduciaries merely because they owed a duty to give disinterested advice?
options: No — a duty to give disinterested advice is not, by itself, sufficient to establish fiduciary status
Yes — any duty to advise without bias automatically creates a fiduciary relationship

testPool.prompt: Besides the fiduciary duty question, Hopcraft's facts also engaged a separate statutory route for challenging the credit agreements. Which?
options: Unfair relationships under Consumer Credit Act 1974, s 140A
Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, s 3
Consumer Rights Act 2015, s 62

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The competing line of authority treated a bribe as giving rise only to a personal claim in debt. The Supreme Court rejected that approach. Where an agent acquires a benefit which was or should have been acquired on behalf of his principal, and which was acquired by the use of the agent's fiduciary position, the agent holds that benefit on constructive trust for his principal. This applies to bribes and secret commissions received by an agent in breach of his fiduciary duty.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where an agent acquires a benefit which was or should have been acquired on behalf of his principal, and which was acquired by the use of the agent's fiduciary position, the agent holds that benefit on constructive trust for his principal.

testPool.prompt: Order the doctrinal development of the remedy for a fiduciary's bribe or secret commission.
items: Attorney General for Hong Kong v Reid treats a bribe as held on constructive trust (Privy Council)
Sinclair Investments v Versailles later restricts recovery to a personal claim in debt
FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital resolves the conflict in the Supreme Court
The proprietary constructive trust analysis is confirmed as the law, and Sinclair is overruled on this point

testPool.prompt: Why does it matter, in practice, whether a claim over a bribe is proprietary (constructive trust) rather than merely personal (debt)?
options: A proprietary claim gives priority over the fiduciary's other creditors and can capture growth in the asset's value
There is no practical difference — both recover the same amount in every case
A personal claim always recovers more because it includes interest automatically

testPool.prompt: A company director, negotiating a supply contract on the company's behalf, is personally offered a stake in the supplier's business as a thank-you for the deal, and accepts without telling the board. The company itself loses nothing and the contract is a commercial success. Is the director liable to account for the stake?
options: Yes — the profit was made by virtue of his fiduciary position, regardless of the company suffering no loss
No — since the company suffered no loss there is nothing to account for
No — because he acted honestly throughout
testPool.explanation: Regal (Hastings) establishes squarely that absence of loss to the principal, and the fiduciary's good faith, do not prevent liability to account for an unauthorised profit made by virtue of the fiduciary position.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor acting for a family trust learns, through that role, of an opportunity to buy a majority stake in a private company partly owned by the trust. With the trustees' general awareness but without every beneficiary's fully informed consent, she buys the stake for herself; the investment strongly benefits the trust's own holding too. Applying Boardman v Phipps, is she liable to account for her personal profit?
options: Yes — she is liable to account absent the fully informed consent of all beneficiaries, even though the trust also benefited
No — because the trust benefited overall, there is no unauthorised profit to account for
No — general awareness by the trustees is sufficient consent
testPool.explanation: Boardman v Phipps holds that benefiting the principal, and keeping trustees broadly informed, is not the same as obtaining fully informed consent from all beneficiaries. Absent that consent, liability to account for the personal profit follows even though the outcome benefited everyone.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that is legally irrelevant to whether the fiduciary is liable to account, according to Regal (Hastings) and Boardman v Phipps.
testPool.scenarioText: A trustee, acting entirely in good faith and with the best interests of the beneficiaries in mind, uses an investment opportunity that arose through his trusteeship to make a personal profit, without obtaining the beneficiaries' fully informed consent.
tappableSpans: investment opportunity that arose through his trusteeship
without obtaining the beneficiaries' fully informed consent
testPool.explanation: Good faith is precisely the fact Regal (Hastings) and Boardman v Phipps treat as irrelevant to liability. What matters is that the profit arose through the fiduciary position and was not authorised by fully informed consent — both of which are present here.

testPool.prompt: Applying Hopcraft v Close Brothers, which relationship is more likely to be found fiduciary?
testPool.scenarioA: An investment manager given full discretion to buy and sell securities on a client's behalf, within a mandate requiring the manager to act solely in the client's interests.
testPool.scenarioB: A retailer's in-house finance assistant who is required by company policy to mention the 'best available' finance option to customers, alongside selling the retailer's own products on ordinary commercial terms.
testPool.explanation: A involves a genuine undertaking of single-minded loyalty and discretion over the client's affairs — the paradigm fiduciary relationship. B mirrors Hopcraft: a duty to mention suitable options within what remains an ordinary commercial, arm's-length selling relationship, which Hopcraft holds is not enough by itself to found fiduciary status.

testPool.prompt: A financial adviser is contractually obliged to act 'in the client's best interests' when recommending products, but earns commission from providers whose products she recommends, disclosed in a general terms document the client never reads. Applying Hopcraft, which is the most accurate view?
options: Fiduciary status is not automatic from the best-interests wording alone; it depends on whether the relationship as a whole shows an undertaking of loyalty going beyond disinterested advice
Any contractual best-interests clause automatically creates fiduciary status
Because commission was disclosed somewhere in the documentation, no legal issue can arise regardless of fiduciary status
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to treat 'best interests' wording as decisive either way — either automatically creating fiduciary status, or (because something was technically disclosed) closing off any issue. Hopcraft requires a closer look at the substance of the relationship: disinterested-advice-type wording alone does not settle fiduciary status either way.

testPool.prompt: Is Hopcraft v Close Brothers Ltd [2025] UKSC 33 a very recent authority relative to when this lesson is being studied?
options: Yes — it is a 2025 Supreme Court decision, materially reshaping this area very recently
No — it is a long-settled nineteenth-century authority

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that 'X owes Y a duty to act in Y's interest in some respect' is, by itself, sufficient to establish that X is Y's fiduciary?
sliderLabels: Not sufficient by itself — more is required (undertaking of loyalty)
Sufficient by itself in every case
testPool.explanation: Mothew and Hopcraft both confirm this is not sufficient by itself. Fiduciary status requires an undertaking of single-minded loyalty going beyond an isolated duty to act with some regard to another's interests within an otherwise ordinary relationship.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in the first four parts of this lesson is assuming good faith, lack of loss, or benefit to the principal can excuse an unauthorised profit — it cannot; the no-profit rule is strict. The most common mistake in the final part is the opposite error: assuming any duty to act with some regard to another's interests makes you their fiduciary. Hopcraft v Close Brothers confirms it does not.
